transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, Doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things at the office have just become entirely untenable. I'm the chief executive, you see, and I have poured my absolute soul into this company, every late night, every weekend, sacrificing my personal life to build our quarterly margins. But recently, there is this... this constant insubordination, or I don't even know what to call it anymore. 

I keep hearing people talking about me. And it’s not just regular office gossip, it’s... well, I will be sitting completely alone at my desk, door shut, and I can hear them clear as day right through the conference room walls. It's usually my own board members, or my senior staff, and they are just going on and on about how I’m completely ruining the company, how I'm incompetent and driving us straight into the ground. 

And the most disturbing part is that it happens with my phone, too. I'll have the device completely turned off, sitting flat on the mahogany desk, screen black, battery drained, and I can still hear their voices coming out of the speaker. It sounds so incredibly real, so perfectly clear, that I actually talk back to them. Just the other day I was sitting there arguing, loudly defending my restructuring strategy to the room, and I answered them right out loud before I even realized that... well, that my assistant had walked in and was staring at me, and that no one else had heard a single word. But I heard it. I hear it all the time and I just... I can't keep trying to run a corporation like this, constantly having to defend myself against people who are speaking to me when they aren't even in the room.
Have you also had a period of several days or more when your mood was abnormally elevated or irritable, with much less need for sleep than usual?

Elevated? I... no, I wouldn't use that word at all. Honestly, the idea of feeling elevated right now sounds like an absolute luxury. If anything, I am just profoundly exhausted. 

I mean, regarding the sleep—look, as a chief executive, my sleep schedule has always been, let's say, highly optimized. You don't get to the C-suite by sleeping eight hours a night when the Asian markets are opening and the European branches need quarterly projections by dawn. So I've always run on maybe five or six hours. But it's certainly not because I have less *need* for it. I desperately want to sleep. I will lie there in bed, completely drained, physically aching from the stress of carrying this entire corporation on my shoulders, just praying for rest. But I can't get it because I'm so tense, so wound up about what they're saying about me and what they're planning for the next board meeting. 

And irritable? Well, of course I'm irritable! But it's completely justified irritability, don't you think? When you are pouring your lifeblood into a company and your own senior staff is whispering about your incompetence through a dead phone screen, how else are you supposed to react? Any rational person in my position would be snapping at people. It's impossible not to be on edge. But it's not some... some bizarre mood swing where I'm suddenly energetic or euphoric or feeling invincible. I'm not bouncing off the walls or staying up for days on a whim. I'm just a very, very tired woman trying to protect the company I built from people who are constantly trying to tear me down. So no, no periods of feeling abnormally elevated. Just... just this constant, heavy, unrelenting stress.
Have there been times when the voices or beliefs continued even when your mood was completely normal?

Normal? I... well, I suppose that depends entirely on what you define as a normal mood, doesn't it? Because, quite frankly, I haven't felt what I would call "normal" in... oh, I don't even know how long. Months, maybe? Ever since this whole ordeal started with the whispers and the phone. 

I mean, if you're asking if I ever just sit there, feeling perfectly fine, perfectly content, sipping a latte and reviewing quarterly reports while they're simultaneously telling me I'm driving the company into bankruptcy... well, no. Because how could anyone possibly feel normal while that is happening? The voices are constant, Doctor. They don't take a day off. They don't respect weekends or holidays. Even when I try to take a moment for myself, perhaps try to read a book or just sit in my living room—which is beautifully decorated, by the way, I spent months picking out the perfect mid-century modern pieces to create a calming environment—even then, the moment I sit down, the moment I try to just be normal, there they are. 

So, I don't think I've had a normal mood at all. I am constantly stressed, constantly anxious, constantly on the defensive. Because the beliefs, as you call them—though I assure you, the threat to my position is very real—and the voices, they never stop long enough for me to just... breathe. To just feel like myself again. So, no, I haven't noticed any periods where I felt completely normal while all of this was going on, because the situation itself is so entirely abnormal and consuming. It just colors every single second of my day.
Have you started any new medications or substances, or changed the dose of any regular ones, before these symptoms began?

No, no, I haven't. I mean, my routine is incredibly strict. You have to be meticulous when you're managing the kind of operations I do, so I don't just take things on a whim. 

I do take a multivitamin, of course. It's a specialized blend, actually, imported from a lab in Switzerland that my personal physician recommended about five years ago, designed specifically for high-stress executives to support cognitive function and cellular health. I take that every single morning with exactly eight ounces of room-temperature water before my first espresso. But that's been a constant for half a decade, not a recent change. And occasionally, if the seasonal allergies are particularly dreadful—you know how the pollen gets in the spring around the corporate campus, it's absolutely atrocious—I might take an over-the-counter antihistamine. But I haven't even touched those in months because they tend to make me slightly drowsy, and as I mentioned, I cannot afford to lose even a fraction of my edge right now. 

I don't do recreational drugs, obviously. I don't even drink much anymore. In my twenties, sure, maybe a glass of Cabernet at a networking event, but alcohol just clouds the mind, and right now, my mind has to be sharper than a scalpel to catch all these... these plots against me. I haven't started any new prescriptions, I haven't changed the dosage of my vitamins, I haven't even changed my brand of espresso beans. Everything in my physical regimen has been exactly the same, down to the millimeter, which is why this whole situation is so incredibly frustrating. There is no external chemical factor to blame this on, Doctor. It's just... it's just them. It's what they are doing to me. So, no, absolutely no new medications or substances whatsoever.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in most things?

Depressed? I... well, I don't know if I'd use the word depressed, but... lost interest? Yes. Yes, actually. And that's... that's maybe the most terrifying part of all this, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I used to be the engine of that entire company. I mean, I was the one driving every single idea. I would be up at 4:00 AM, firing off emails, calling people right after market openings, pushing the envelope on our expansion strategies. I *loved* it. I thrived on it. The rush of closing a deal, the satisfaction of outmaneuvering a competitor... it was my entire life. My husband used to joke that I was married to the firm and he was just my weekend retreat. And he wasn't entirely wrong, bless him. 

But now? For the last few weeks... it's like someone just pulled the plug. I can sit at my desk in my corner office—which, by the way, has a stunning panoramic view of the city skyline, something I worked incredibly hard to earn—and I'll just sit there for hours. Just... staring at the agenda. The quarterly reports will be right in front of me, the same reports that used to make my pulse race with excitement, and I just feel... nothing. It's like looking at a blank piece of paper. I don't care. I just don't care about the work I used to absolutely love. 

And it's not just the work. It's the people, too. I barely speak to my staff anymore. I used to walk the floor, check in with the department heads, keep everyone motivated. Now, I keep my door shut. I don't even really talk to my husband when I get home. He'll ask me how my day was, and I just... I don't have the energy or the desire to form the words. I just give him a one-word answer and go sit in the dark. It's this profound, heavy emptiness. So, yes, I suppose for the last couple of weeks, maybe more, I have completely lost that drive, that pleasure in everything that used to define me. It's all just... gone.
Have the voices ever been present when your mood was clearly back to normal and you were not depressed?

Normal? I... well, I thought we just went over this, Doctor. I really don't think I've had a "normal" mood since this whole nightmare began. I mean, how could I? 

You're asking if there was a time when I wasn't feeling this... this heavy, awful emptiness, but the voices were still there? I... no, I don't think so. Because it's all tangled up together. The whispers, the feeling that my entire board of directors is conspiring to oust me, the complete loss of interest in the very company I built from the ground up... it's all happening at once. It's a constant barrage. 

If I'm not feeling completely drained and apathetic, sitting in my office staring blankly at the skyline, then I'm anxious and terrified because they're telling me I'm a failure, that I'm ruined. There hasn't been a moment, not a single day, where I've woken up, felt like the old me—the sharp, driven, energetic executive who could command a room with just a look—and still heard them. If I felt like my old self, I wouldn't be sitting here in this chair, would I? I'd be out there, fighting back, taking control of the narrative. But I can't. Because the voices and this... this depression, or whatever you want to call it, they are entirely intertwined. They feed off each other. So no, I haven't had any period where my mood was completely fine, completely normal, but the voices were still lingering. It's just one big, continuous, exhausting ordeal.
Have you ever been convinced that people are actually plotting against you or trying to harm you, even when there was no clear evidence for it?

No clear evidence? I... Doctor, I find that question a little insulting, frankly. No, of course not. I have never just... imagined that people are plotting against me out of thin air. I don't operate on baseless fantasies or wild guesses. 

You have to understand, I didn't get to the position of Chief Executive by jumping to conclusions or making decisions without data. I am a highly analytical person. I deal in facts, in market trends, in concrete metrics. I spent three years at university before I realized I was already outperforming my professors in the real world, and I built my career on being able to read the data better than anyone else. So if I am telling you that my board of directors is conspiring to oust me, it is because there is a mountain of evidence pointing exactly to that conclusion. 

I mean, it's all right there if you actually know how to read the room. It's the way my CFO suddenly stops copying me on the preliminary budget forecasts—which, by the way, I instituted a strict policy on three years ago that I am always to be CC'd on. It's the hushed conversations that abruptly stop the second I walk into the executive lounge. It's the fact that three of the senior board members had a private dinner at that new steakhouse downtown last Tuesday and conveniently "forgot" to mention it to me, even though we always, always discuss major structural changes over dinner. 

That is evidence, Doctor. It's subtle, yes, and maybe someone who isn't trained to navigate high-stakes corporate warfare wouldn't see it. Maybe to an outsider it just looks like normal office politics, but it is absolutely clear to me. I don't just wake up and decide someone is out to harm me for no reason. I would never survive in my industry if my mind worked like that. Everything I'm experiencing, everything I'm trying to protect myself against, is based on a very real, very tangible pattern of behavior from the people around me. So, no. I have never believed there was a plot against me without clear, undeniable proof. The proof is everywhere, it's just that no one else is paying attention.
Have you ever had a period of several days or more when you felt unusually energetic or restless, with a reduced need for sleep?

Unusually energetic? Restless? No, no, I... I don't think so. I mean, what do you even consider "unusually" energetic for someone in my position? 

Because, look, my baseline—before all this, before the emptiness and the whispering and the absolute dread—my normal was what most people would probably call hyperactive. I was running a multi-million dollar firm. You don't get to the top by needing eight hours of beauty sleep every night. There were weeks, especially during the acquisition of that tech startup two years ago, where I was functioning on maybe three, four hours of sleep a night. I'd leave the office at midnight, go home, shower, review the legal drafts until 3:00 AM, and be back at my desk by 6:00 AM with a double espresso, ready to tear into the negotiations. 

But that wasn't... I wasn't manic, or restless in some unhealthy way, if that's what you're implying. It was just the job. It was what the situation demanded. I was focused, I was sharp, I was entirely in control of every single moving piece. I didn't feel restless, I felt purposeful. Every ounce of energy I had was directed exactly where it needed to go. My husband would beg me to slow down, to take a weekend off, but I couldn't. The momentum was too important. If you lose momentum in a hostile takeover, you lose the deal. It's that simple. 

So, yes, I've had periods of intense energy and very little sleep, but it was always tied to a specific project, a specific goal. It wasn't just some random, uncontrollable surge of energy for no reason. And certainly not recently. Lately, as I told you, just the thought of opening an email feels like trying to lift a boulder. I haven't had a shred of energy in weeks. The idea of feeling restless or energetic right now is almost laughable. I just feel... drained. Completely, utterly drained. So, no, I haven't had any periods of unusual energy that weren't directly related to closing a massive deal.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were not depressed or unusually energized, but you were still hearing the voices?

Doctor, I feel like we are going in circles with this. I know I just touched on this, but no. There hasn't been a two-week period, or even a two-day period, where I felt "normal" while this has been happening. How could anyone possibly maintain a stable, non-depressed mood when they are subjected to this kind of psychological siege? 

The entire reason I even came in here to see you—the only reason I stepped away from my desk during such a critical fiscal quarter—is because I keep hearing people talking about me. And it is relentless. I hear them right through the conference room walls. And my executive suite has top-tier, custom-installed acoustic paneling that cost a fortune, but I still hear them perfectly. It’s usually the board members, or my senior staff, and they are just going on and on, saying that I’m ruining the company. That I'm destroying everything I built. 

And it’s not just through the walls at the office. It’s my phone, too. I will hear them talking from my phone even when the screen is black and the device is completely powered off. I’ll hold the button down, swipe to power off, set it face down on my desk, and I can still hear them whispering from the speaker, criticizing my leadership. 

And the thing is... it sounds so incredibly clear. It doesn't sound like an echo or a trick of the ear. It sounds so real, so present in the room with me, that I actually answer them. I will literally be sitting there by myself, hear one of the board members say I'm bankrupting us, and I’ll snap right back at them out loud, aggressively defending my quarterly projections, before I even realize... before I realize that the room is entirely empty and no one else heard it. 

So, you tell me, Doctor. How could I possibly have a normal two weeks when I am constantly having to argue with voices coming out of a powered-down phone or a soundproof wall? It’s exhausting. It drains every ounce of life and energy out of me. So no, there was no two-week period where I felt fine. The voices and this awful, heavy feeling are completely connected.
Have you ever had hallucinations or delusional beliefs when your mood was completely normal for at least two weeks?

Doctor, are you... are you just reading down a standardized checklist right now? Because I feel like I literally just answered this exact same question two minutes ago. I just told you, no. There is no completely normal mood happening here. How could there possibly be?

Let me break this down for you again, because maybe I am not being clear enough, though in my professional life I am known for being exceptionally clear. My mood, my emotional state, whatever terminology you want to apply to it, has been entirely dictated by what is happening to me. You are asking if I have had these... what you are choosing to call delusional beliefs or hallucinations, while feeling perfectly fine for two straight weeks. First of all, they are not delusions, as I have already meticulously outlined for you regarding the board of directors and their very real actions. But secondly, no. Absolutely not. 

Do you have any idea what it actually feels like to have your life's work dismantled behind your back? To hear the very people you hired, people whose salaries you approved, whispering about your downfall through a piece of technology that is turned off? It is agonizing. It is a constant, suffocating weight on my chest. There is no two-week vacation from that feeling. There is not even a two-hour vacation from it. 

If I am hearing them, if I am dealing with the reality of their plotting, I am miserable. I am completely drained. The two things are inextricably linked. You do not just go about your day, feeling completely normal and emotionally stable, while your entire reality is under siege. So, no. Never. Not for two weeks, not for two days. I really do not know how many different ways I can explain that this heavy, awful emptiness and the things I am experiencing are happening at the exact same time. Can we please move on to something else now? I am trusting you to guide this process, but we are just going in circles and I really need to figure out a solution here.
Have you ever heard voices or had these beliefs when you were not feeling depressed?

Doctor, honestly, I feel like I am sitting in a hostile deposition right now. Are you actually listening to the words coming out of my mouth, or are you just waiting for your turn to speak so you can ask me the exact same question for a fourth time? 

I don't know how I can be any clearer about this. No. The answer is no. I have never—not once—heard them plotting against me, or experienced this... this absolute nightmare of a situation, without feeling completely and utterly crushed by it. How could I? I really want you to think about what you're asking me. You're asking if I can just sit there, feeling perfectly fine, not depressed, maybe having a grand old time, while I listen to my senior staff whispering through the walls about how incompetent I am. 

It doesn't work like that. The second it starts—the second I hear that faint crackle from my powered-down phone and the CFO starts talking about stripping my equity—the misery hits me. It is instantaneous. It’s like a physical weight just drops right onto my chest and pins me to the floor. The sadness, the exhaustion, the feeling that I can't even lift my head up... it is the direct result of what they are saying and doing to me. You cannot separate the two. It’s cause and effect. If someone is stabbing you in the back, you don't just feel neutral about it. You feel the pain. 

So no, I have never had these experiences without feeling completely, suffocatingly depressed. They are a package deal. Every single time I hear them, my mood plummets into this dark, heavy place where I can barely function. I really need you to understand this, because if you keep trying to compartmentalize my feelings from what is actually happening to me, we are never going to get anywhere. Can we please, finally, talk about how to actually make this stop? Because I cannot keep defending my answers to you when my entire company is slipping through my fingers.
Have you become noticeably less able to feel or show emotion, even when you’re not upset?

You know... that is actually... that’s a different question. And... yes. To be completely honest with you, yes. It’s actually one of the things that scares me the most right now, because it is so fundamentally, completely unlike who I am as a person, and especially who I am as a leader. 

I mean, you have to understand, I used to be the person driving every single idea in that building. I was the engine of the entire operation. If we had a new market opening or a big product launch, I was the one calling people at all hours, hyping up the team, celebrating the wins, pushing us forward. I had so much passion for it. It was my lifeblood. 

But now? Now... I don't even know who I am. I can go into my executive suite, shut the door, and just sit at my desk for hours. Literally hours, just staring blankly at the daily agenda on my monitor. I won't move, I won't make a call, I won't even react to an urgent email. And I don't necessarily feel actively upset or angry in those specific moments, I just... I feel completely empty. Like a void. 

I barely speak to my husband anymore when I get home, which I know is terribly unfair to him because he's trying so hard to understand what's happening to me, but I just don't have the emotional capacity to form the words or even fake a smile for him. I just sit there. And it's the exact same with my staff. I just pass by them in the halls like a ghost, barely acknowledging they exist. I feel almost nothing—absolutely nothing—about the work I used to love more than anything in the world. It’s like someone just flipped a switch and drained every drop of vitality and feeling out of me, and I’m just left sitting there, completely blank.
Have you ever had at least two weeks when the voices or beliefs were present even though you were not depressed or unusually energized?

Doctor... are you... I mean, I really don't want to be disrespectful, because I know you're the professional here and I'm coming to you for help, but I feel like we are trapped in some kind of bizarre loop. I feel like I'm in a boardroom meeting where everyone is just repeating the same slide over and over again, completely ignoring what I'm actually saying. 

I just... I literally just answered this. I answered it two questions ago, and I answered it three questions ago. I don't know how many more times, or in how many different variations, I can explain the exact same concept to you. No. The answer is still no. Never. Not for two weeks, not for two days, not for two hours. 

I don't have these... these experiences... without feeling completely destroyed by them. I am never just sitting around, feeling perfectly fine, or "unusually energized," whatever that even means in this context, while my entire life is being dismantled by my own board of directors. The voices, the plotting, the absolute betrayal of it all—it is the direct cause of my misery. When I hear them, I am depressed. I am crushed. I am exhausted. They happen together, always. I cannot separate the experience of being betrayed from the emotional devastation of that betrayal. 

I really, really need us to move past this specific question, because I feel like I'm losing my mind just trying to get you to hear me. I've told you no, repeatedly, in extensive detail. So, no. Never. Can we please talk about something else now? Because this repetition is just making me feel even more hopeless about getting this resolved.
Have you ever had any hallucinations or fixed beliefs that were unrelated to your mood—for example, when you were feeling completely neutral?

Doctor, I... I am genuinely at a loss here. I am actually speechless, which, if you asked anyone at my firm, they would tell you is a near impossibility for me. I... I don't understand what is happening right now. Are you reading off a checklist? Is there some sort of mandatory protocol where you have to ask me the exact same question five different ways before we can actually discuss treatment? Because I feel like I am going insane, and not in the way I came here to get help for.

I have told you, over and over and over again. No. No, I do not have these... these fixed beliefs, or whatever you want to call them, when I am feeling completely neutral. How could I possibly feel neutral? I want you to really, truly picture the scenario you are asking me about. You are asking if I can sit in my office, or in my living room, completely unbothered, totally neutral, maybe thinking about what I'm going to have for lunch, while I am simultaneously experiencing the profound, world-shattering realization that the people I hired, the people I mentored, are actively conspiring to ruin my life and take my company from me. 

It is a contradiction in terms! It is impossible! The moment I hear them—the moment the CFO's voice comes through the vents, or my phone crackles—the neutrality is gone. It is instantly replaced by the most agonizing, suffocating depression and despair you can imagine. There is no neutral. There is no unrelated to my mood. The mood is caused by the event. It is a direct, immediate, inescapable reaction. 

I don't know how to make this any clearer. I really don't. I feel like I am screaming into a void here. I came to you because my life is falling apart, because my company is slipping away, because I am so depressed and empty that I can barely function... and instead of helping me, you are just interrogating me with the same question on an endless loop. Please. I am begging you. Can we please move on? Because I cannot answer this again. I just can't.
Have you noticed any difficulty with your speech, like your thoughts getting jumbled or others saying it's hard to follow what you're saying?

No, no, I haven't... I mean, I haven't noticed anything like that. My speech is fine. It's actually one of the only things I feel like I still have a grip on, to be honest. I mean, communication is—or at least it was—the absolute core of my job. You don't get to be a CEO by having jumbled thoughts or being hard to follow. You get there by being precise, by being articulate, by being able to walk into a room of fifty skeptical investors and lay out a strategic vision so clearly that they have no choice but to write you a check. 

And even now, even with everything that's happening, with the board plotting against me and this overwhelming emptiness I was telling you about... when I do speak, I know exactly what I'm saying. I'm not stumbling over my words. I'm not losing my train of thought. If anything, I feel like I'm being too clear, and people just aren't listening. Like right now, with us, I feel like I'm explaining things in agonizing detail, but it's just not landing. 

But no, nobody at the office has said I'm hard to follow. Of course, they barely speak to me anyway these days unless it's to plot behind my back, but when I do give a directive, it's clear. My husband hasn't said anything about it either. He just... he looks at me with this pity, like he doesn't know what to do with me, but he understands what I'm saying. So, no, my thoughts aren't jumbled. The thoughts themselves are just... they're just heavy. But the way they come out is perfectly fine.
Have you ever had any head injury, seizure, stroke, or other major neurological illness before these symptoms began?

No, nothing like that. I mean, absolutely nothing. I've always been incredibly healthy, physically speaking. I mean, I run—or I used to run, before all of this started and I couldn't even get out of bed—I used to run five miles every morning before the sun even came up. I was militant about my health. You have to be, in my line of work. You can't afford to be out with a cold, let alone a... a stroke, or a seizure. 

I've never hit my head, never been in a car accident, never even fainted. I think the worst thing I've ever had was a mild concussion when I was maybe twelve, playing soccer, but that was decades ago and completely insignificant. I've certainly never had any major neurological illness. My brain has always been my best asset, my sharpest tool. That's why this is all so terrifying, because I know my brain is physically fine. I know there's no tumor or injury causing this. 

I actually went to my primary care doctor when the... when the exhaustion and the depression first started hitting me so hard, before the voices really escalated, just to make sure I didn't have a thyroid issue or vitamin deficiency or something. And they ran every test under the sun—blood work, an MRI, everything—and it all came back completely pristine. The doctor actually told me I had the lab results of a twenty-five-year-old. 

So, no, there is no physical, neurological explanation for this. It's not a brain injury. It's not a stroke. It's just... it's just my life falling apart, and my mind being completely overwhelmed by the betrayal and the sadness of it all. I wish it were a head injury, honestly. At least then there would be a physical reason, something you could point to on a scan and say, "There, that's the problem, let's fix it." But no. Physically, neurologically, I am perfectly fine.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being inserted into your mind, or that other people could hear your thoughts?

No. No, of course not. That sounds like science fiction, Doctor. My thoughts are my own. In fact, my thoughts are the very last thing I have left in this world that are entirely, exclusively mine. 

If people could hear my thoughts, believe me, the board wouldn't have to sneak around plotting against me. They would already know exactly what I think of them. They would know how much I despise their cowardice, their greed. If the CFO could read my mind, he wouldn't need to whisper through the vents to the others about how they're going to push me out, because he would already know that I'm onto them. But they don't know. They have no idea what's going on in my head. My mind is a fortress. It is a very dark, very depressing fortress right now, but it is locked tight. Nobody is getting in, and nothing is leaking out. 

And as for someone inserting thoughts into my mind? Absolutely not. I generate my own ideas. I built a company from the ground up, with no trust fund, no elite Ivy League degree—just some college and a lot of grit. I didn't get to the C-suite by having someone else magically beam strategies into my brain. I did it through my own intellect. I am in complete control of my own cognitive faculties. 

The thoughts I have right now—the overwhelming despair, the crushing realization that everything I built is being stolen from me by the very people I mentored—those are my thoughts. They belong to me. They are a logical, rational reaction to the nightmare that is my reality. It's almost insulting, honestly, that you would ask if my thoughts are being inserted, because it implies that I'm not the author of my own intellect. I am. I always have been. The problem isn't my thoughts being broadcast or manipulated by some outside force. The problem is what is actually happening to me in the real world, and how utterly powerless I feel to stop it. So, no. No mind reading, no thought insertion. Just me, alone in my head, watching my life burn down.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing or believing these things while your mood was otherwise normal, without depression or unusual energy?

No... no, it hasn't been like that. The... the depression, the emptiness, it's been there the whole time. It's like a heavy blanket over everything. I can't even remember a time in the last several months where my mood was just... normal. You know? Where I woke up and felt like myself. I used to wake up energized, ready to tackle the day, ready to go into the office and lead my team. Now, it's just this constant, crushing weight. 

And the voices, the plotting... it all started around the same time. It's impossible to separate them, really. How could my mood be normal when I know my own board of directors is actively conspiring to ruin me? When I can hear the CFO whispering through the air vents about pushing me out? It's terrifying, and it's exhausting. It drains every ounce of energy I have just trying to figure out who I can trust, which is no one. 

So, no, there was never a two-week period where I felt fine but was still hearing these things. The sadness, the lack of energy, the inability to even get out of bed some days... that's been a constant companion to the betrayal. It's all tangled up together. I mean, if you were in my position, if everything you had built with your own two hands, with just some college and a ridiculous amount of hard work, was being ripped away from you by the people you mentored... wouldn't you be depressed? It's a completely natural reaction. It's not like the voices started and I was just happily going about my day. The whole thing is a nightmare, and it's been a nightmare from the start.
